questions.question: Which question does Descriptive Analytics answer?
options: Why did this happen?
What happened?
What will happen?
How do we fix it?
questions.explanation: Descriptive analytics (the core of BI) summarizes the past or present state of the business, e.g. 'Sales were $1.2M last month.' Diagnostic analytics asks 'why,' predictive asks 'what will happen,' and prescriptive asks 'how do we optimize it' — those last two belong to data science, not classic BI.

questions.question: In the BI Stack, which layer is responsible for catching a problem like 'yesterday's data sync silently failed' before a stakeholder notices a wrong number on a dashboard?
options: BI Consumption (the dashboard tool)
Observability
Semantic Layer
Source Systems
questions.explanation: Observability tools (e.g., dbt tests, Monte Carlo, Elementary) monitor for late, missing, or anomalous data across the pipeline. The dashboard layer just renders whatever numbers it's given — it has no way to know the underlying data is stale or wrong unless an observability layer flags it first.

questions.question: A BrightCart dashboard shows 'Revenue dropped to $0 today.' Following the BI Stack mental model, what should you check FIRST?
options: Whether the chart's color scheme is misleading
Whether the Extract & Load job actually ran and brought in new rows
Whether the CEO misread the chart
Whether to switch BI tools entirely
questions.explanation: A sudden drop to exactly $0 is almost always a pipeline failure (an Extract & Load job silently stopped) rather than a real business event or a math/visualization error. Checking upstream layers first is faster than re-auditing the dashboard's formulas.

questions.question: Using BrightCart's events sample (7 distinct users: 101-107, where 101, 102, 103, 106 have a purchase event), what is the Weekly Active User count under Definition C ('Active' = completed a purchase)?
questions.explanation: Definition C counts only users with a 'purchase' event_type. In the sample, users 101, 102, 103, and 106 each have at least one purchase event — that is 4 distinct users. Definitions A (login) and B (key action) would return different, larger counts because they include browsing-only behavior.

questions.question: Why does the SQL query for WAU use `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` instead of `COUNT(user_id)`?
options: DISTINCT makes the query run faster on large tables
Without DISTINCT, a user with multiple qualifying events would be counted once per event, inflating the user count
DISTINCT is required syntax in all SQL dialects
COUNT(user_id) would throw an error on NULL values
questions.explanation: If User 101 has 2 purchase events in the week, COUNT(user_id) would count them as 2, even though it's 1 unique person. COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) collapses repeats so the metric measures unique users, not total actions — the entire point of an 'Active Users' metric.

questions.question: In a metric contract for 'Weekly Active User,' what does the 'late-arriving events' field address?
options: How fast the dashboard loads in the browser
The fact that mobile app events may sync up to 72 hours after they occur, so the metric must be marked 'provisional' until finalized
How long the CEO has to read the dashboard
Which time zone the developer lives in
questions.explanation: Offline mobile queueing means an event recorded on a phone might not reach the events table for hours or days. A rigorous metric contract acknowledges this lag, labels recent weeks as 'provisional,' and only finalizes numbers once the late-arrival window has passed — otherwise the same week's WAU number would keep silently changing.

questions.question: Why is a central Data Warehouse important for a 'Single Source of Truth'?
options: It is cheaper than Excel
It ensures everyone uses the same data and definitions, avoiding conflicting reports
It automatically predicts the future
It replaces the need for analysts
questions.explanation: Consistency, not cost or automation, is the primary value driver of a warehouse. When Marketing and Finance both query the same certified tables with the same metric definitions, they stop arriving at the boardroom with different numbers for 'customers.'

questions.question: What is the 'Semantic Layer' in the BI stack, and why does it matter for metric contracts?
options: It is just a marketing term for any dashboard
It is where business metrics like 'Revenue' are defined exactly once so every BI tool computes them identically
It is the layer where raw data first enters the warehouse
It is a synonym for the data lake
questions.explanation: Without a semantic layer, each analyst might re-derive 'Revenue' slightly differently in each tool (one excludes refunds, another doesn't), reintroducing the exact single-source-of-truth problem the metric contract was designed to prevent. The semantic layer (e.g., dbt Semantic Layer, LookML) centralizes the definition once.
